title: Aston Martin F1 crisis deepens with engine battery shortage at 2026 Australian GP
content:
MELBOURNE, Australia — Aston Martin’s ongoing Formula 1 struggles have deepened ahead of the 2026 season-opening Australian Grand Prix, as the team now has just two engine batteries left for its cars.

After a miserable preseason testing period where it struggled with both the reliability and performance of its new car, Aston looked poised to complete limited mileage in Australia this weekend.

Team principal Adrian Newey then revealed on Thursday that drivers Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll are currently unable to complete even half a race distance due to fears of permanent nerve damage from the significant vibrations in the car.

This stems from the Honda engine, which is also damaging the battery. The problem became so severe during the final preseason test in Bahrain last month that Aston had to stop its program after just six laps because it lacked battery parts to complete the test.

Alonso took no part in opening practice at Albert Park on Friday due to another suspected engine problem, while Stroll managed just three laps before his session was cut short for the same reason. Both drivers were able to get out on the track within the first 15 minutes of the second practice.

Speaking at the FIA news conference on Friday, Newey revealed that Aston is still facing a critical battery parts shortage due to the underlying vibration problem on the car, leaving each car with just one functioning battery.

“We are short on batteries,” said Newey. “We’ve only got two batteries left, the two that are in the car. If we lose one of those, then it’s obviously a big problem. We’ve got to be very careful on how we use the batteries.”

Should Aston suffer any further serious setbacks with the two remaining batteries, it would put it at risk of being unable to take part in Sunday’s race. Newey said Aston had started the weekend with four working batteries.

“Given our rate of battery damage, it’s quite a scary place to be in,” Newey said. “Obviously, we’re hopeful that we can get through the weekend and start two cars (in the race), and so on and so forth. But it’s very difficult to be concrete about that at the moment.”

Asked if it was possible to fly more batteries to Melbourne for Aston to use, Newey replied, “Unfortunately not, there aren’t any.”

Following its struggles in testing and amid its parts shortage, Honda completed additional engine testing at its factory in Japan over the past week, with a view to introducing a series of countermeasures to address the vibration problem in Australia.

Although Newey said there had been “very clear action” from Honda to ease the issue, he said it was “not going to be a quick fix.” Until Honda resolves the reliability issue, it will not be able to focus on the engine’s performance.

“At the moment, this vibration issue is sucking all energy in every area,” Newey said. “(Even) emotionally. I mean, our mechanics were up until four o’clock this morning. They’re on their knees.

“The factory has been offering a lot of support. It’s something we really need to try to get on top of as quickly as possible.”

During the news conference, Newey spoke of the struggles Honda had faced when rebuilding its engine project after temporarily quitting F1 in 2020, only to reverse its decision in early 2023 to link up with Aston Martin for 2026.

Newey claimed that a lot of the new engineers working on the Honda F1 engine project were “fresh to F1,” meaning the manufacturer lacked the experience it had when it was working with Red Bull in the previous F1 rules era, as well as now facing spending limitations under the championship’s cost cap.

This was not in place for engine builders when Honda last turned around a bad program with McLaren in 2015-2017 to become successful with Red Bull from 2021.

Newey also revealed that Aston only became aware of the inexperience within Honda’s F1 program late last year during a meeting in Tokyo to discuss rumors that Honda was behind its targets for the first race.
